lead: Recognition is the act of deciding which pattern class a measured feature vector belongs to. An object is measured, the measurements become numbers, and a classifier compares those numbers with what it learned from labelled examples. This exists because a raw image is too rich to compare directly; a short vector makes the decision cheap and repeatable. It is used in postal address reading, fruit grading, signature checking and medical screening. The same steps appear in modern deep models: an image becomes a vector, and a head names the class.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 for segmentation and descriptors, and Unit 1 for pixels and neighbourhoods.

blocks.text: A pattern is the set of measurements taken from one object. A pattern class, written ω₁, ω₂, …, ω_W, is a set of patterns that share the property we care about. W is the number of classes. One tomato is a pattern; all ripe tomatoes form one class. The class is not one sample.

The measurements are placed in a feature vector x = (x₁, x₂, …, xₙ). Each xᵢ is a number with a unit: area in pixels, mean intensity, perimeter in pixels, or compactness (unitless). n is the dimension. The set of all possible x is the feature space, usually Rⁿ. A recogniser maps x to one label from the W classes.

blocks.where: x is the feature vector; xᵢ is the i-th measured feature; n is the number of features, so the vector has n dimensions.

blocks.text: Descriptors provide the raw material. Regional descriptors include area, perimeter, compactness and eccentricity. Topological descriptors include number of holes H, number of connected components C, and Euler number E = C − H. These are not the classifier; they are the numbers fed to it.

blocks.where: E is the Euler number; C is the number of connected components; H is the number of holes in the object.

blocks.text: Recognisers fall into two families. Decision-theoretic methods use the numeric vector and a decision function. Structural methods use relations between parts, usually a string or a graph of sub-patterns. A printed word can be a string of characters; a face can be a graph of eyes, nose and mouth.

A training set is a group of samples with known class labels. A test set is a separate group used after training. Supervised learning uses the labels to fix a rule. Unsupervised learning groups unlabelled samples into clusters, and a human later names each cluster. Accuracy on the training set can be optimistic; the test set estimates how the rule works on new objects.

Two classes are separable if some rule puts every sample on the correct side. In one dimension this is a threshold. In two dimensions it is a line. In n dimensions it is a hyperplane. Classes are linearly separable if a straight boundary separates all samples. Overlap means no perfect rule exists, so we measure error rate and cost.

Feature numbers must be chosen with care. Area in pixels and mean intensity have different ranges, and one may hide the other unless scaled. If the descriptor misses the property that separates the classes, no classifier can recover it. The decision rules themselves are in 6.2.

A form is scanned, binarised, and segmented into lines and characters. For each character we compute features: area, bounding-box width and height, number of holes, and counts of foreground pixels in fixed zones. These numbers form x. The classes are the letters and digits needed by the form. Training samples come from several fonts and scans; test samples come from unseen forms. A decision rule from 6.2 then assigns a label. A structural check can help: a character is a graph of strokes, and “8” has two holes, “0” has one, and “1” has none.

This case is used in postal sorting, cheque reading and form digitisation. Most errors come from broken strokes, touching characters and poor segmentation. A segmentation error appears later as a classification error, so the descriptor step and the classifier must be judged together.

examples.question: A tomato-grading unit sorts fruit into ripe (ω₁) and unripe (ω₂) using two features: mean red intensity R and area A in pixels. Training samples are ω₁: (180, 40), (190, 42), (175, 38) and ω₂: (110, 41), (120, 39), (105, 43). (a) Write the pattern vector. (b) How many classes and what is n? (c) Does R alone separate the classes? Give a threshold. (d) Does A add anything here?
steps: The pattern vector is x = (R, A). R is mean red intensity and A is area in pixels. Here W = 2 classes and n = 2 features.
Ripe R values are 180, 190, 175. Their minimum is 175 and maximum is 190. Unripe R values are 110, 120, 105. Their minimum is 105 and maximum is 120.
The largest unripe R is 120. The smallest ripe R is 175. Since 120 < 175, no sample lies between them. Any threshold T with 120 < T < 175 separates all six samples.
Take the midpoint: T = (120 + 175) / 2 = 147.5. Rule: call the fruit ripe if R > 147.5, else unripe. All six training samples are correct.

Ripe area values are 40, 42, 38, giving range 38 to 42 pixels. Unripe area values are 41, 39, 43, giving range 39 to 43 pixels. The ranges overlap from 39 to 42, so A alone cannot separate the classes and is redundant for these samples.
In the (R, A) plane the boundary R = 147.5 is a vertical line. It separates the two classes, so the classes are linearly separable.
examples.answer: x = (R, A); W = 2 classes; n = 2 features; R alone separates them, with threshold R = 147.5 (ripe if R > 147.5); area A is redundant here because its class ranges overlap.
examples.check:
ripe = [(180,40),(190,42),(175,38)]
unripe = [(110,41),(120,39),(105,43)]
W = 2
n = 2
min_ripe = min(r for r,a in ripe)
max_unripe = max(r for r,a in unripe)
threshold = (min_ripe + max_unripe) / 2
print(W)
print(n)
print(min_ripe)
print(max_unripe)
print(threshold)

traps: A pattern class is a set of samples that share a property; it is not one sample.

A pattern is the set of measurements from one object, and the pattern vector (also called the feature vector) is those measurements written as an ordered list x = (x₁, …, xₙ). Do not confuse a pattern (one sample) with a pattern class (the set of samples sharing a property).
n is the number of features, and W is the number of classes. They are not the same symbol or the same count.

A feature is useful if it helps separate the classes, alone or together with other features. In the tomato example area is dropped because R alone already separates the classes and the area ranges overlap.
Segmentation and description come before classification. A descriptor builds x; the classifier only assigns the label.

quiz.q: Define pattern and pattern class. In ω₁, ω₂, …, ω_W, what does W count?
quiz.a: A pattern is the set of measurements taken from one object. A pattern class is a set of patterns sharing a property. W is the number of classes.

quiz.q: A feature vector has n = 5. What is the feature space and what is its dimension?
quiz.a: The feature space is the set of all possible feature vectors, here R⁵. Its dimension is 5.

quiz.q: Why report accuracy on a test set instead of only on the training set?
quiz.a: Training accuracy can be too high because the rule has already seen those samples. A test set contains unseen samples, so it estimates how the rule behaves on new objects.

quiz.q: Class A has one feature values {4, 6, 8}. Class B has {1, 2, 3}. Find a threshold that separates them and state the rule.
quiz.a: Largest B is 3 and smallest A is 4. Midpoint is (3 + 4) / 2 = 3.5. Rule: class A if f > 3.5, else class B. All samples are correct.

quiz.q: A character region has C = 1 connected component and H = 2 holes. Find its Euler number E.
In the tomato example, area ranges overlap but R separates the classes. Which feature should be kept and why?
quiz.a: Keep R, because a threshold on R separates all training samples. Area overlaps between 39 and 42 pixels, so it adds no separating power for these samples and may be dropped.

quiz.q: Why may a structural representation suit signature recognition better than a fixed-length vector?
quiz.a: A signature is a sequence of strokes, so the order and relation between parts carry identity. A string or graph can encode stroke order and connections. A fixed-length vector of global shape may lose that order and confuse signatures with similar overall shape.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern recognition replaces hand-built descriptors with learned embeddings, where a network maps an image to a vector and distance means similarity. Open-set recognition asks a model to say “unknown” instead of forcing one of W classes. Self-supervised pretraining learns features without labels and is common before fine-tuning on a small labelled set. Search terms: metric learning, contrastive loss, open-set recognition, foundation models for vision.
